velden.waarde: Tilburg School of Humanities and Digital Sciences
Caution: this information is subject to change

Knowledge:

•    how social spaces, relationships, and practices are digitally mediated (analytical thinking)
•    some of the main terminology, theoretical perspectives and disciplinary boundaries of digital culture, e.g. globalization, mediatization, datafication and digitalization
•    academic and other writing conventions, genres, and practices

Skills:

•    identify and evaluate relevant academic literature (research skills)
•    organize, present and discuss claims made about digital culture to a range of target audiences
•    apply theoretical frameworks to interpret and analyse digital culture
•    work in groups (social/group skills/planning and organization skills) 

Character:

By addressing timely societal issues and by zooming in on academic debates and media representations, the course promotes critical and creative thinking and digital and academic citizenship.

It seems reasonable to expect that the digitalization of life - who we are and can be online, what we do with digital media and vice versa - will continue to intensify in the coming years. This implies that the degree to which we integrate digital technology into much of what we do will also grow exponentially. For example, AI technologies (whatever we may think of them) are likely to shape and feed into social practices such as buying insurance, designing media or learning to drive a car. As a result, people’s everyday practices, their cultural identities, and their representations online will shift, often imperceptibly. Understanding how we deal – critically and creatively – with such socio-cultural changes triggered by ongoing globalization and mediatization is the exercise we shall undertake in this course. 

This course will follow up on Exploring Digital Culture and continue to introduce you to the study of digital cultures, focusing specifically on critical and creative approaches. You will read about and familiarize yourself with core theoretical concepts which we will use as a common language to explore and research culturally significant practices online and to express the big and small ideas you need to explain these practices in a clear and precise way. You will also learn how to share your knowledge with an audience. In other words, this course ticks two important boxes: academic socialization (read to write) and foundational learning (core concepts paradigms). As a bonus, it might even be fun and interesting!

Observable performance expected of students:

  • contribute to and lead class discussions
  • critically assess and annotate academic literature
  • attend classes and make deadlines
  • stay on top of the weekly readings

Note: This course is open to students who have taken the Exploring Digital Cultures -  in semester 1.
